paras: The alleged election-day intimidation at Sumter, South Carolina, refers to reports on November 2, 1880, that armed Democrats crowded the polls in Sumter County, kept Republican voters away, and ejected federal deputy marshals. A private despatch to Senator Blaine went further, describing a riot and smashed ballot boxes, while dispatches to South Carolina papers said the election passed off quietly. No deaths or injuries were reported, and the dispute continued in Samuel Lee's contest of the First District congressional seat.

Sumter County lay in South Carolina's First Congressional District, where Samuel Lee, a former probate judge of the county, ran as the Republican candidate against the Democratic incumbent, John S. Richardson. The Washington National Republican later wrote that Sumter Democrats had driven Lee out of the state in 1878 and that he returned in 1879 after receiving 'assurances of protection'.

On election day Lee, signing as a United States deputy marshal, telegraphed Jay A. Hubbell of the Republican Congressional Committee that armed Democrats crowded the polls and would not let Republicans reach them. He added that Republican poll managers refused to hold the election, that the marshals' authority was defied and they were expelled from the polls, and that 'No election can be held in this county.' A separate private despatch to Senator Blaine, reported in Maine the next day, said a riot was raging, that Democrats had driven the U.S. supervisors and 'the negroes' from the polls, and that all the ballot boxes had been smashed.

Dispatches from Sumter to the Columbia Daily Register and South Carolina papers gave a different picture. They reported 2,000 to 2,500 Black men gathered in town from across the county, 'armed with pistols' according to the late bulletin, with no disturbance and order kept by the municipal authorities. By 11 p.m. the same correspondent reported that Republicans were ahead in the count, though 'gross irregularities' were charged, and that deputy marshals at the polls had made no arrests.

Sumter was one of only three South Carolina counties the Democrats did not carry, according to the Abbeville Press and Banner. In December Lee served notice that he would contest Richardson's seat, alleging stuffed ballot boxes at Lynchburg, Maysville, Shiloh and Privateer, a poll at Stateburg that managers never opened, and obstruction of supervisors and deputy marshals across the district. By March 1881 a correspondent wrote that testimony in the contest showed Democrats had refused to open polls in four Republican counties, Sumter among them. Lee's notice did not repeat the claims of a riot or smashed ballot boxes, and no report of arrests or prosecutions over the Sumter polls appears in the coverage.

Republican papers printed Lee's telegram on election day itself, the Washington Evening Star under the headline 'Reported Prevention of a Fair Election in Sumter County' and the Carson City Morning Appeal under 'The Democrats Step the Election by Force.' At the same time the Register's brief 'no disturbance' special from Sumter ran without comment among state returns in Washington, Knoxville, St. Paul and Chicago.

South Carolina weeklies in Winnsboro, Anderson and Yorkville described the day as quiet but placed the threat on armed 'negroes' who 'spoke defiantly of the Democrats', and called Republicans 'Radicals'. When Lee pressed his contest, the Edgefield Advertiser headlined the item 'The Negro Sam Lee Opens the Contest,' while the National Republican defended him against 'Democratic thugs.'

Whether any violence occurred is contested: Lee's telegram and the Blaine despatch allege force at the polls, while the Sumter dispatches to the state press report a quiet election. The two sides also disagree over who was armed, Lee naming 'armed democrats' and the Democratic dispatches naming about 2,000 Black men with pistols. The claim of smashed ballot boxes rests on the single unsigned despatch to Blaine.

accounts.label: Deputy Marshal Lee's telegram
accounts.gist: Armed Democrats crowded the polls and kept Republicans away, Republican poll managers refused to hold the election, and deputy marshals were defied and ejected; no election could be held in the county.

accounts.label: Private despatch to Senator Blaine
accounts.gist: A riot was raging at Sumter; Democrats drove the U.S. supervisors and Black voters from the polls and smashed all the ballot boxes.

accounts.label: Columbia Daily Register special
accounts.gist: Twenty-five hundred Black people had gathered in Sumter from across the county, with no disturbance so far, and the county looked safe for the Democrats.

accounts.label: Sumter dispatch to South Carolina papers
accounts.gist: The election passed off quietly; about 2,000 Black men armed with pistols were massed in town all day, order was kept by the municipal authorities, and Republicans were ahead amid charges of 'gross irregularities'.

accounts.label: Lee's notice of contest
accounts.gist: Ballot boxes were stuffed at four Sumter precincts, the Stateburg poll was not opened, and supervisors and marshals were obstructed throughout the district.

framing.detail: Republican papers ran Lee's telegram under 'Reported Prevention of a Fair Election in Sumter County' (Evening Star) and 'The Democrats Step the Election by Force' (Morning Appeal).
Northern and western dailies carried the Columbia Register's 'no disturbance' special among state returns without comment.
South Carolina papers reported quiet while describing 2,000 'negroes' armed with pistols who 'spoke defiantly of the Democrats', and called Republicans 'Radicals'.
